messages.body_plain:
Hi Roy,

You imported your datasets separately without supplying a projection argument, so they all have independent, automated projections. I have added an error message when overlap is called on distributions with different projections. This is why the overlaps are all too high.
Especially, with this data, you need to use ctmm.select instead of ctmm.fit. The error was caused by multiplication of infinite variance with zero sensitivity, which equals NaN, because the model was bad with infinite uncertainty on some parameters that didn't have support.
I fixed the error (even with a bad model), so that it will return appropriate CIs and not crash.

The patches should be up on GitHub by tomorrow: which you will be able to install via devtools::install_github("ctmm-initiative/ctmm"). Please report any further issues.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hey Chris,

I am working with telemetry data of 18 white storks which have their breeding area in Loburg, Germany. The data features a default temporal interval of 5 mins which is, due to bad weather conditions, sometimes decreased to 20 minutes or even one hour intervals. Furthermore, every night, the devices shut down for 6 hours between around 8pm and 2am.

With the help of the ctmm package I would like to reconstruct the movement path in order to derive a more realistic value (including confidence intervals) of the time spent in certain areas of interest at each day during the breeding season in one specific year. The migration periods (autumn and spring) are already excluded from the data.

I attended the Animove summerschool in 2017 and followed the basic steps for data pre-processing provided in your introductory lesson. However, using the stork data I encountered several problems:

The data comes in movebank format featuring the necessary columns and naming conventions (location.long, location.lat, timestamp, etc) as well as the additional column eobs.horizontal.accuracy.estimate.

I tried the pre-processing workflow with different individuals, as a reproducible example however, I sent you the data of one month (April) from a single individual due to privacy reasons.

Step 1: Convert data to Telemetry object

The conversion seems to work but I am not sure whether the error estimate column is automatically recognized or if I have to specify it somehow when creating the telemetry object? I only found the UERE variable but don't know how to include it there. Here is my code example:

# convert dataframe with WGS84 coordinates to to Telemetry object with ETRS89 projection

StorkTele<- as.telemetry(Storks_samp, timezone ="UTC", timeformat= "%F %T",

projection = CRS('+proj=laea +lat_0=52 +lon_0=10 +x_0=4321000 +y_0=3210000 +ellps=GRS80 +units=m +no_defs'))

Step 2: Data cleaning

In a next step I tried to identify outliers using the outlie() function and got a dataframe with two columns (distance, speed).

OUT <- outlie(StorkTele)

Looking at the resulting values I noticed, that quite often, when the birds flew distances larger than zero between two consecutive locations the speed estimate remained zero. Intuitively, that seems to be wrong for me. Do you have an explanation for that?

Step 3: Inspect autocorrelation

In order to inspect the autocorrelation structure of my data I created and plotted a correlogram(). The creation worked but the plot() command produced the following warning:

CORR <- correlogram(StorkTele)

plot(CORR)

Warning message:
In atanh(SVF) : NaNs produced

… and resulted in an erroneous plot: (see Attachement_1_Correlogram_Error)

To inspect what causes the NaNs I did the following:

NaN <- cbind(CORR$SVF, atanh(CORR$SVF))

The problem seems to come from the CORR$SVF. The latter results in values slightly larger than 1 and produces the NaNs when calculating the hyperbolic tangent. Looking at my input coordinates I was wondering if that is a result from the number of decimal places of my coordinates taken into account when creating the telemetry object or if anything is seriously wrong with my data? Would you have an idea where the issue comes from and how I can fix it?

Thank you very much in advance for your help.

Greetings,

Ines

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ines,

I hope you are well. A lot of this material is going to be in an upcoming paper that I am finalizing now. Some of this is presently in vignette('error') <https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html>.

1) This appears to be e-obs data and it imports with an error column which you can see from the head() or names() of the telemetry object, where you have HDOP and VAR.xy columns. You can also see from plot() that there are error circles of different size.

The calibration for e-obs data comes from Scott LaPoint's fisher calibration data, and I should warn that the collars that did not function well did not have the same calibration parameters (UEREs). You can use your own calibration data to overwrite this UERE value, following vignette('error') <https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html>.

2) The speed & distance estimators here are error informed, with the speed estimates derived from point-to-point distances (so they represent an upper bound on the true speed). These estimates consider the erroneous location observations as being distributed around the true locations by the specified error. As error inflates the "distance" between erroneous locations, accounting for error will estimate a smaller quantity. Interestingly, when the error is above a certain threshold, the point estimate of the true distance is zero. However, the full posterior distribution (CIs) includes more than zero. I do not return this information, though, because it is some work to calculate and I don't see the use for it in outlier detection.

3) correlogram() <https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/residuals.html> in ctmm is only for residuals. Other data will break assumptions in the math. If you want to check the residuals assuming an IID model, you can fit an IID model and then run that and the data through the residuals() function, and then the output residuals through correlogram(). If you want to inspect the autocorrelation structure of data, then variogram() function is better because its estimator is unbiased. Tell me if you have any issues with that.

Best,
Chris

Hi Chris,

The basic OUF model might fit okay to those, even though it isn't a perfect match (I'm iffy on 3). You should try fitting and compare the empirical variograms and fitted models. The best home-range estimate is more than likely going to be AKDE based on the best trend and autocorrelation model (which we refer to as the "movement model"). You would want to give caveats when your best movement model doesn't seem very good in an absolute sense. But the best movement model will almost never be IID, which is what you assume when doing conventional KDE or MCP.

In some cases of dispersal or migration, you can segment the data to break it up into stationary pieces. This is a stop gap measure until better movement models are developed.

There are periodic models in the package, vignette("periodogram") <https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/periodogram.html>, but I have not yet coded them to work with akde() as this is very complex.

Best,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hey Chris,

Within my study I tried to simulate White Storks movement path of different behavioral clusters (consecutive locations of the same behavioral class). I need to do this in order to derive the time spent in certain areas of interest during a specific activity. For that purpose, I followed the steps discussed with you during the AniMove 2017 using a test data set of one individual. The data was captured during breeding season (April to August) with a default temporal interval of 5 mins which is, due to bad weather conditions, sometimes decreased to 20 minutes or even one hour intervals. Furthermore, every night, the device shuts down for 6 hours between around 8pm and 2am. In the following, the applied steps are explained in detail:

a) Derivation of behavioral clusters (each behavioral cluster should at least contain 5 consecutive locations)

Data$Behavior_Clust

b) Mean centering of behavioral clusters: The mean x and mean y location of all points of a clusterx are subtracted from each x and y point-location of a clusterx

library(tidyverse)

Bouts_centered ← Data %>%

group_by(Behavior_Clust) %>%

mutate(location.long_centered = location.long – mean(location.long)

(location.lat_centered = location.lat – mean(locationlat)

Hi Ines,

Just from first pass:

1) Fig. 1 looks crazy. If you put all the foraging data together before fitting the model and ran simulations from that model, the variance of the simulations should not dwarf the variance of the collective foraging data, so I would assume something has gone wrong here. Figs. 1&2 should be tighter to the data than Figs. 7&8. The y-axis on Figs. 3&4 is 100x smaller than the y-axis on Figs.5&6, which makes sense, but this should lead to the first simulations being 10x tighter to the clusters.

In other situations, where things look more reasonable, during the larger gaps, the simulation will become less correlated to the data and more similar to the Gaussian model. With the occurrence distribution (?occurrence <https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/occurrence.html>) there are arguments dt.max and cor.min that you can use to avoid completely filling in gaps that are too large (otherwise you just get a big blob). Its not documented, but these arguments (dt.max and cor.min) also work on the conditional simulations. So you could run simulate() with argument dt.max=5 %#% 'min' and this would only simulate trajectories but so far out from the data, only completely filling in gaps of 5 minutes. You aren't to the point where you need to worry about this nuance, though.

With the simulations not exactly running through the data, this is appropriate if the model contains error. Then the sampled locations are taken to be erroneous and the degree to which the simulations converge on the data is determined by the size of the errors. If you set error=FALSE, then the simulations should go exactly through the data. Fig. 2 looks crazy, though, and I assume something else has gone wrong here.

2) e-obs data should be imported and calibrated from Scott LaPoint's calibration data. If you have your own calibration data from the same model tags, that would likely be preferable. With Scott's calibration data, I found the e-obs error estimates to be highly predictive, but the calibration constants were not consistent on collars that did not perform well.

Because the e-obs data get calibrated by as.telemetry (assuming everything went well) your error<-5 command doesn't do anything different from error<-TRUE, as the data already contain error variances that do not need to be fit. Overwriting the calibration requires using uere()<- on the data, but be careful to note that this is telling you how to interpret the e-obs error estimates (I treat them as an HDOP value) and not setting all error standard deviations to 5 meters, which would also require deleting the HDOP column. Some of these details are covered in vignette('error') <https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html>.

3) I would fit, either to the mean detrended foraging data or to the individual foraging periods depending on whether or not you can assume the foraging behavior to be homogeneous and whether or not you have sufficient data per foraging event. Either way should get you something much tighter and more appropriate than fitting to the entire dataset without detrending.

I am in the middle of coding up some models that fit better with tiny tracks and can update you when I have that working. I will not have true CPF models for some time.

Regarding the 6 hour gap at night, I would probably skip the gaps that large with the arguments I mentioned above.

I'll try to look into this more carefully in a few days or so. I am in the middle of coding and grant preparation right now.

Best,
Chris

Hi Ines,

2) e-obs and ARGOS data should be automatically calibrated during as.telemetry(). The trend I found with Scott's calibration data was that e-obs devices that were missing many fixes had a much smaller UERE.

4.1) The second (higher resolution?) variogram plot looks possibly okay to me. For your analysis, you just want the first few lags to match (up to how large of gaps you will simulate through). If the sampling is irregular, you might consider bumping up the res argument until the variogram stops changing, or using fast=FALSE. This decreases some of the distortion from irregular sampling, but its not possible to remove all of it.  Remaining distortion you can examine by simulating tracks under the same irregular sampling schedule and looking at their resulting variograms.

4.2) How much IID data your autocorrelated data is worth for estimating the mean, the home-range area, and the RMS speed.

4.3) I recommend doing everything manually like you have for the first animal, and then automating (interactive=FALSE in ctmm.guess) everything in a way that saves the comparison plots to look over at the end. For 25 animals, I don't think 25 plots would be terrible to look at.

Best,
Chris
